tools.name: exec

format.definition:
start: pragma_source | plain_source
pragma_source: PRAGMA_LINE NEWLINE SOURCE
plain_source: SOURCE

PRAGMA_LINE: /[ \t]*\/\/ @exec:[^\r\n]*/
NEWLINE: /\r?\n/
SOURCE: /[\s\S]+/

tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.

tools.name: request_user_input
tools.description: Request user input for one to three short questions and wait for the response. This tool is only available in Plan mode.

questions.description: Questions to show the user. Prefer 1 and do not exceed 3

header.description: Short header label shown in the UI (12 or fewer chars).

options.description: Provide 2-3 mutually exclusive choices. Put the recommended option first and suffix its label with "(Recommended)". Do not include an "Other" option in this list; the client will add a free-form "Other" option automatically.

description.description: One short sentence explaining impact/tradeoff if selected.

question.description: Single-sentence prompt shown to the user.

tools.name: request_user_input_async
tools.description: Ask the user one or more questions during ongoing work. Use this tool only to request missing information, preferences, constraints, clarification, or approval. The tool returns immediately without ending the turn or waiting for a reply; any reply arrives asynchronously as a new user message. Keep questions concise, self-contained, and easy to understand, using a level of detail appropriate to the user and task. The UI always allows a free-text answer, including when suggested options are provided. A preselected option is not submitted automatically.

questions.description: One or more self-contained questions to present together, in display order.

options.description: Suggested answers, in display order. Put the recommended answer first; the first option is preselected by default. The user can select one option or enter a free-text answer. Do not include an Other option or a free-text placeholder; the UI provides free-text input automatically. Omit options for a free-text-only question.

title.description: The complete question shown to the user, including any context needed to answer it.

tools.name: send_message_to_user_async
tools.description: Send a concise message that needs the user's attention during ongoing work. The tool returns immediately without ending the turn or waiting for a reply; any reply arrives asynchronously as a new user message. Use this tool to report a critical blocker or a finding that may change the task's direction, or to answer a user question or status request received while work is still in progress. Use this tool when a message needs the user's immediate attention; use commentary for routine progress and intermediate context. Use clear formatting, such as bolding questions, to make requests easy to notice and answer.

message.description: The concise question or update to send to the user.

tools.name: clock
tools.description: Tools for reading and waiting on time.

tools.name: sleep
tools.description: Pause execution for a specified duration. The sleep ends early when new input arrives for the active turn. Returns the elapsed wall-clock time.

duration_ms.description: How long to sleep in milliseconds. Must be between 1 and 43200000.

tools.name: collaboration
tools.description: Tools for spawning and managing sub-agents.

tools.name: followup_task
tools.description: Send a follow-up task to an existing non-root target agent and trigger a turn if it is idle. If the target is already running, deliver the task promptly at message boundaries while sampling, or after the pending tool call completes.

message.description: Message text to send to the target agent.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to send a follow-up task to (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: interrupt_agent
tools.description: Interrupt an agent's current turn, if any, and return its previous status. The agent remains available for messages and follow-up tasks.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to interrupt (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List live agents in the current root thread tree. Optionally filter by task-path prefix.

path_prefix.description: Task-path prefix filter without a trailing slash. Omit to list all live agents.

tools.name: send_message
tools.description: Send a message to an existing agent. The message will be delivered promptly. Does not trigger a new turn.

message.description: Message text to queue on the target agent.

target.description: Relative or canonical task name to message (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: spawn_agent
tools.description:
Available model overrides (optional; inherited parent model is preferred):
- `gpt-6.2-sol`: Fast, go-to model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6.2-astra`: Our most capable model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6.1-terra`: Efficient model that excels at visual understanding and computer use. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.1-sol`: Previous generation model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6-astra`: Previous generation model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6-sol`: Legacy model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-luna`: Fast and affordable model for easier tasks. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.6-sol`: Legacy model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.6-terra`: Legacy balanced model for agentic coding. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.6-luna`: Legacy fast model for simpler tasks. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.5`: Legacy coding model. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh. Service tiers: priority.
        Spawns an agent to work on the specified task. If your current task is `/root/task1` and you spawn_agent with task_name "task_3" the agent will have canonical task name `/root/task1/task_3`.
You are then able to refer to this agent as `task_3` or `/root/task1/task_3` interchangeably. However an agent `/root/task2/task_3` would only be able to communicate with this agent via its canonical name `/root/task1/task_3`.
The spawned agent will have the same tools as you and the ability to spawn its own subagents.

It will be able to send you and other running agents messages, and its final answer will be provided to you when it finishes.
The new agent's canonical task name will be provided to it along with the message.

Note that passing `fork_turns="none"` will not pass any surrounding context to the spawned subagent, which may cause the agent to lack the context it needs to complete its task, whereas `fork_turns="all"` will provide the subagent with all surrounding context.

fork_turns.description: Parent history to inherit. Defaults to `all`; use `none` to start without parent history. Only `all` and `none` are supported.

message.description: Initial plain-text task for the new agent.

model.description: Model override for the new agent. Omit unless an explicit override is needed.

reasoning_effort.description: Reasoning effort override for the new agent. Omit to inherit the parent effort.

task_name.description: Task name for the new agent. Use lowercase letters, digits, and underscores.

tools.name: wait_agent
tools.description: Wait for a mailbox update from any live agent, including queued messages and final-status notifications. The wait also ends early when new user input is steered into the active turn. Does not return the content; returns either a summary of which agents have updates (if any), an interruption summary for steered input, or a timeout summary if no activity arrives before the deadline.

timeout_ms.description: Timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000, min 10000, max 3600000.

tools.name: mcp__cua_repl
tools.description: UI automation through cua_repl using the initialized cua API.

tools.name: js
tools.description:
Control native apps or browsers on the user’s computer by reading or operating UI. Prefer purpose-built skills, connectors, APIs, or CLIs when available.

On the first invocation of `cua_repl`, or after resetting it, execute exactly one of the API calls shown below, optionally assigning its result to a variable. Do not add other API calls, waits, or snapshots to that invocation.
The tool result will include documentation and, when creating or selecting a tab or selecting an app, its initial UI state. Selecting a browser does not open a tab. Read that result before continuing.
Use only APIs described in the tool instructions or returned documentation.

When you need an inventory of available apps, browsers, and tabs, get a snapshot of all enabled surfaces. Otherwise, use the relevant entry point below:

```javascript
await cua.getState();
```

Use the first matching browser control option from the user's request:

For a tab @-mention (`mention=tab-v1`):
Pass the complete `plugin://...` URL to get the referenced tab.

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab({ mention: tabMentionUrl });
```

For an existing tab identified by URL in browser context (including the current IAB tab):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab({ url }, { browser: browserId });
```

Known tab ID (`tabId` or `providerTabId`) and browser (name or browser @-mention):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab(tabId, { browser: browserId });
```

To open a URL in the in-app browser (`@Browser`):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.createBrowserTab("iab", url, { visible: boolean });
```

To open a URL in another named browser: pass its name directly; do not call `getBrowser` first.

```javascript
let tab = await cua.createBrowserTab(browserName, url, browserOptions);
```

Known URL, only when the user has not specified a browser by name or @-mention:

```javascript
let browser = await cua.getBrowser({ url });
```

Browser IDs and options:

- `"mcpapps"`: use `cua.getBrowser({ id: "mcpapps" })` for existing full-screen MCP Apps in the task’s side panel.
- `"iab"` (in-app browser): in `createBrowserTab`, use `visible: true` to show the browser; `false` to keep it hidden.
- `"dot"` (Dot): use only when present in browser inventory. It accesses tabs on Dot's active main thread. `cua.getTab(tabId, { browser: "dot" })` selects an existing tab. `cua.createBrowserTab("dot", url, { visible: boolean })` creates one with the same visibility options as `"iab"`.
- `"chrome"` (@Chrome), `"edge"` (@Edge): pass a short, emoji-prefixed `sessionName` (e.g. `"🔎 Task"`) to `createBrowserTab` when starting a task.

If the user specifies an app to use, get the app by name, bundle ID, or path:

```javascript
let app = await cua.getApp("Example App");
```

To add other content to the tool result, use `nodeRepl.write(value)` for text or other values and `await nodeRepl.emitImage(image)` for images. The APIs listed above already display their documentation or UI state; do not wrap their results in `write` or `emitImage`.

If your context begins with a summary of an existing computer use task, call `await cua.rewriteDocumentation()` before continuing the computer use task to ensure you have a complete view of the necessary documentation.

Each `cua_repl.js` call opens or continues a browser activity. Keep consecutive calls together. The activity stays open across messages until you emit completion commentary.

**Manual takeover takes priority over the table below.** For a required manual browser step, call the documented takeover API before asking the user to act, unless takeover is already pending. Explain the required step in your final reply. Tab marking alone does not transfer control. While waiting for the user to finish and return control, emit no completion and make no CUA calls, even when answering side questions. The takeover API returning does not end this wait. When the user returns or unblocks you, resume browser work and apply the table. If they cancel, replace, or no longer need the browser work, close the activity before answering, even without another CUA call.

Completion is a standalone assistant commentary message containing only `::browser-complete{title="<headline>"}`. Never put it in a tool call or final reply. Use 3–6 words starting with a past-tense verb to describe the observed outcome. Omit identifiers.

After a user cancels pending browser work: commentary `::browser-complete{title="Stopped browser work"}`, then the final acknowledgement. No browser call is needed.

For an open browser activity:

| Next action                                   | Required output order                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Another CUA call                              | Continue without completion.                                                              |
| A non-CUA tool, final reply, or chat question | Finish required tab marking, emit completion, then take that action in the same response. |

With no open activity, emit no completion. Later CUA use requires a fresh completion at the next table boundary.

If you need a one-time sign-in code, information, or confirmation from the user, follow the table and ask in chat. One-time code entry alone does not require takeover. This tool is part of plugin `unified-computer-use`.

code.description: JavaScript to execute using the initialized cua_repl runtime.

timeout_ms.description: Optional execution timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000 (30 seconds) when omitted.

title.description: Short user-facing description of what this code block is doing. Prefer a few words in present-progressive form, such as 'Checking the mobile layout' or 'Comparing prices', over imperative or past-tense titles.

tools.name: js_reset
tools.description: Reset the persistent cua_repl JavaScript session. All JavaScript bindings are discarded. The next cua_repl.js call initializes a fresh runtime for the enabled surfaces. This does not close browser tabs or native apps, or erase their state. This tool is part of plugin `unified-computer-use`.

## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/Users/alexcallow/.agents/skills`
- `r1` = `/Users/alexcallow/.codex/skills/.system`
- `r2` = `/Users/alexcallow/.codex/plugins/cache/egm/egm/0.1.1/skills`
- `r3` = `/Users/alexcallow/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-bundled`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r1/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: API first-timers, Codex/Work Q&A. If the user already has an OpenAI API integration, skip this skill for API questions and use the developer docs. Read this skill before answering how Codex or ChatGPT Work behaves, where to find a feature, or how to configure or troubleshoot this app or coding agent. This includes conversation history, model and cache behavior, instruction precedence, permissions, and tool availability. Use for API onboarding only when the user is connecting to the OpenAI API for the first time. Skip action requests, such as scheduling an automation, and tasks fully answered by supplied text or data. (file: r1/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r1/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r1/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
- apollo-client: Guide for building React applications with Apollo Client 4.x. Use this skill when: (1) setting up Apollo Client in a React project, (2) writing GraphQL queries or mutations with hooks, (3) configuring caching or cache policies, (4) managing local state with reactive variables, (5) troubleshooting Apollo Client errors or performance issues. (file: r0/apollo-client/SKILL.md)
- built-in-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Codex desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Codex's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. It is not for Codex in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (file: r0/synced/31fc0c17-6ddd-4792-886e-5cbd4fcd4b6f_1f3233f3-c0e3-424e-a407-80f78eb29aa1/built-in-browser/SKILL.md)
- chrome-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses Codex in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. - code-review: Review the changes since a fixed point (commit, branch, tag, or merge-base) along two axes — Standards (does the code follow this repo's documented coding standards?) and Spec (does the code match what the originating issue/PRD asked for?). Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side. Use when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes, or asks to "review since X". (file: r0/code-review/SKILL.md)

# Frame Inventory

Monorepo scaffold for the frame-inventory take-home exercise.

## System Overview

The Next.js page calls the Spring Boot health endpoint through a same-origin rewrite. Docker Compose runs both modules alongside PostgreSQL, OpenSearch, and OpenSearch Dashboards. The exercise provides a legacy export in `data/inventory_frame.csv` and describes the inventory features in `INSTRUCTIONS.md`.

Bring the whole stack up with one command.

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

## Subdirectories & System Boundaries

- [Application source](./src/README.md) contains the Java 21 and Spring Boot 3.5 backend and the Next.js, React 19, and TypeScript frontend.
- [Design system](./design-system/README.md) contains the prototype, sample frame data, and visual conventions for the exercise.

## Services

`docker compose up` starts the following services.

| Service               | Host port | Container port | Notes                                                  |
|-----------------------|-----------|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------|

export COMPOSE_FILE="$PWD/docker-compose.yml:$verification_dir/compose.yml"
cat > "$verification_dir/compose.yml" <<'YAML'
services:
  backend:
    container_name: !reset null
  postgres:
    container_name: !reset null

export COMPOSE_FILE="$PWD/docker-compose.yml:$verification_dir/compose.yml"
cat > "$verification_dir/compose.yml" <<'YAML'
services:
  backend:
    container_name: !reset null
  postgres:
    container_name: !reset null
    ports: !reset []
YAML
trap 'docker compose down --volumes' EXIT
just migrate
just migrate
docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U app -d frames -At -c 'SELECT version, success FROM flyway_schema_history' > "$verification_dir/schema-history"
cat "$verification_dir/schema-history"
test "$(cat "$verification_dir/schema-history")" = '1|t'

- `just down` stops the stack and keeps its data volumes.

- `just migrate` starts PostgreSQL, waits for it to become healthy, and applies pending Flyway migrations in a one-off backend container.

Verified against a temporary database that `just migrate` applies V1 on the first run and exits cleanly on rerun.

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Suggested infrastructure for the Frame Inventory exercise.
#
# This compose file is a starting point, not a requirement. You are free to
# swap any of these services for tooling you prefer (a different database,
# search engine, message broker, hosting model, etc.) as long as the final
# stack still runs end-to-end with a single command.
#
# If you do choose to use the services provided here, pick ONE of the two
# datastores for your domain data — either `mongodb` or `postgres`,
# not both. Remove the service you do not need (and its volume) so the
# stack reflects the design you actually built.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

services:
  backend:
    build:
      context: ./src/backend
    container_name: frame-inventory-backend
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: docker
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/frames
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      opensearch:
        condition: service_started
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  frontend:
    build:
      context: ./src/frontend
    container_name: frame-inventory-frontend
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      BACKEND_URL: http://backend:8080
    volumes:
      - ./src/frontend/src:/app/src
      - ./src/frontend/public:/app/public
    depends_on:
      - backend
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  postgres:
    image: postgres:18.6
    container_name: frame-inventory-postgres
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: frames
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U \"$$POSTGRES_USER\" -d \"$$POSTGRES_DB\""]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 15
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  opensearch:
    image: opensearchproject/opensearch:2.18.0
    container_name: frame-inventory-opensearch
    environment:
      cluster.name: frame-inventory-cluster
      node.name: opensearch
      discovery.type: single-node
      bootstrap.memory_lock: "true"
      OPENSEARCH_JAVA_OPTS: "-Xms512m -Xmx512m"
      DISABLE_SECURITY_PLUGIN: "true"
      DISABLE_INSTALL_DEMO_CONFIG: "true"
    ulimits:
      memlock:
        soft: -1
        hard: -1
      nofile:
        soft: 65536
        hard: 65536
    ports:
      - "9200:9200"
      - "9600:9600"
    volumes:
      - opensearch-data:/usr/share/opensearch/data
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  opensearch-dashboards:
    image: opensearchproject/opensearch-dashboards:2.18.0
    container_name: frame-inventory-opensearch-dashboards
    ports:
      - "5601:5601"
    environment:
      OPENSEARCH_HOSTS: '["http://opensearch:9200"]'
      DISABLE_SECURITY_DASHBOARDS_PLUGIN: "true"
    depends_on:
      - opensearch
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

volumes:
  postgres-data:
  opensearch-data:

networks:
  frame-inventory:
    driver: bridge
# List available commands.
default:
    @just --list

# Build and start the full stack in the foreground.
up:
    docker compose up --build

# Stop and remove the stack's containers and network.
down:
    docker compose down

# Run any Docker Compose command, for example `just compose logs -f backend`.
[positional-arguments]
compose *args:
    docker compose "$@"

# Apply pending Flyway migrations using the backend's database configuration.
migrate:
    docker compose up -d --wait postgres
    docker compose run --build --rm --no-deps backend --spring.main.web-application-type=none
server:
  port: 8080

spring:
  application:
    name: frame-inventory-backend
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/frames
    username: app
    password: app

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info
plugins {
    id 'java'
    id 'org.springframework.boot' version '3.5.14'
    id 'io.spring.dependency-management' version '1.1.6'
}

group = 'com.global.ct.frameinventory'
version = '0.0.1-SNAPSHOT'

java {
    toolchain {
        languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21)
    }
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web'
    implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-actuator'
    implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-jdbc'

**Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.**

When editing existing code:

* Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
* Don't refactor things that aren't broken.

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:

* "Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"
* "Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"
* "Refactor X" → "Ensure unit and gRPC integration tests pass before and after"

[Step] → verify: [check]
[Step] → verify: [check]

## 6. Build, Protobuf & Test Commands

* **Maven:**

  * Run unit & integration tests: `./mvnw test`

## 7. SOLID Principles in Spring Boot & gRPC

### S — Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

*A class should have one, and only one, reason to change.*

* **gRPC Adapters (`*ImplBase` subclasses) & Controllers:** Responsible *only* for handling transport concerns—unwrapping and validating incoming Protobuf messages (or HTTP requests), delegating to an application service/use case, mapping the domain result back to a Protobuf response, and completing the `StreamObserver` (`onNext()` / `onCompleted()`). Never put business logic or direct repository calls in a gRPC service implementation.
* **Services (`@Service`):** Contain pure business logic and transaction boundaries (`@Transactional`). Break down large "God Services" into smaller, cohesive, domain-focused services or use cases.
* **Repositories (`@Repository`):** Responsible *only* for data persistence and retrieval. Do not include business rules in custom queries or repository implementations.
* **Mappers:** Use dedicated mapper classes or MapStruct to convert between Protobuf messages, Domain models, and JPA Entities. Do not bloat entities, stubs, or services with mapping logic.

### O — Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

*Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification.*

* **Strategy Pattern with Spring DI:** When multiple implementations or business rule variants exist (e.g., payment processing, notification channels, discount calculations), avoid large `if-else` or `switch` statements. Define a common interface and inject a `List<StrategyInterface>` or `Map<String, StrategyInterface>` via Spring's dependency injection to resolve implementations dynamically.
* **gRPC Interceptors (`ServerInterceptor`):** Handle cross-cutting transport concerns (authentication, logging, distributed tracing, and global exception-to-`io.grpc.Status` translation) via Spring-managed `ServerInterceptor` beans rather than repetitive `try-catch` blocks inside RPC methods.
* **Domain Events:** Use Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher` and `@EventListener` (or `@TransactionalEventListener`) to decouple side effects (e.g., sending an email after user registration) from core business flows.

### L — Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

*Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program.*

* **Contract Adherence:** Implementations of an interface must honor the expected behavior, preconditions, and postconditions of the interface.
* **No Unsupported Operations:** Never implement an interface method by throwing `UnsupportedOperationException`. If a class cannot fulfill the entire interface contract, the interface is too broad (see ISP).
* **Exception Consistency:** Subclasses or interface implementations should not throw unexpected checked or runtime exceptions that violate the caller's expectations of the base type.

### I — Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

*Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use.*

* **Focused `.proto` Contracts:** Keep gRPC service definitions granular and domain-aligned (e.g., `UserQueryService`, `UserCommandService`) rather than monolithic `.proto` files with dozens of unrelated RPCs.
* **Role-Specific Java Interfaces:** Avoid bloated Java interfaces. Split them into focused interfaces based on client needs (e.g., `UserQueryUseCase`, `UserRegistrationUseCase`).
* **Repository Interfaces:** Do not blindly extend `JpaRepository` if a consumer only needs read access. Consider defining custom base repository interfaces (e.g., `ReadOnlyRepository<T, ID>`) exposing only `findById` and `findAll`.

### D — Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

*High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.*

* **Strict Boundary Isolation (Protobuf & JPA):** Never leak generated Protobuf classes (`*Request`, `*Response`) or JPA `@Entity` classes into the core `application` or `domain` layers. Map both Protobuf messages and JPA Entities to/from pure Java domain models (`record` or domain classes) at the outer adapter boundaries.
* **Depend on Abstractions:** Core domain/business services must depend on interfaces (ports) rather than concrete infrastructure classes (adapters) like external gRPC stubs (`*BlockingStub`), REST clients, or third-party SDKs.

## 8. gRPC & Protocol Buffers Guidelines

* **Contract-First Development:** Place all `.proto` definitions in `src/main/proto/` organized by domain and version (e.g., `src/main/proto/user/v1/user.proto`).
* **Proto Options:** Always include `option java_multiple_files = true;` and a clear `option java_package = "...";` so generated classes are clean and modular. Never manually modify generated Java stub files under `target/generated-sources/` or `build/generated/`.
* **Protobuf Defaults & Presence:** Remember that `proto3` scalar fields default to zero-values (`0`, `""`, `false`) and cannot be `null`. Use the `optional` keyword or wrapper types in `.proto` when distinguishing between unset and default values is required by business logic.
* **Error Mapping:** Throw domain-specific exceptions in the service layer (e.g., `ResourceNotFoundException`, `InvalidArgumentDomainException`) and translate them centrally into appropriate `io.grpc.Status` codes (`Status.NOT_FOUND`, `Status.INVALID_ARGUMENT`, etc.) at the gRPC interceptor/advice boundary.

## 9. Recommended Package Structure

Organize packages by **feature/domain** using Hexagonal / Clean Architecture boundaries so transport (gRPC/REST) and persistence remain completely decoupled from business logic:

```text
src/main
├── proto
│   └── feature/v1              # .proto contract definitions
└── java/com/example/project
    ├── common                  # Shared utilities, interceptors, base configs
    │   ├── grpc                # Global gRPC ServerInterceptors & Status exception mappers
    │   └── config              # Security, gRPC, and Jackson configurations
    └── feature                 # e.g., order, user, payment
        ├── adapter             # Inbound & Outbound Adapters
        │   ├── in.grpc         # gRPC *ImplBase services & Protobuf Mappers
        │   ├── in.web          # (Optional) @RestController & HTTP DTOs
        │   └── out.persistence # JPA Entities, Spring Data Repositories, Entity Mappers
        ├── application         # @Service classes, Use Case implementations, Event Listeners
        └── domain              # Pure Java Domain Models, Records, Ports (Interfaces), Domain Exceptions
```

## 10. Coding Standards & Transactions

* **Transactions:** Place `@Transactional` on application service methods that modify state. Use `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` for query-only service methods to optimize database performance.
* **Validation:** Validate incoming Protobuf requests immediately at the gRPC adapter boundary (or via `protovalidate` / custom validators) before invoking domain use cases. Enforce business invariants inside domain models.
* **Immutability:** Prefer `final` fields in all Spring beans and use Java `record` types for all internal commands, queries, domain value objects, and `@ConfigurationProperties`.

## 11. Testing Requirements

### Unit & Persistence Tests

* **Unit Tests:** Every new `@Service` and domain component must have fast, isolated unit tests using **JUnit 5** and **Mockito** (no Spring context or gRPC server loaded).
* **Persistence Tests:** Use `@DataJpaTest` and **Testcontainers** for repository integration tests requiring a real database.
* **Assertions:** Prefer **AssertJ** (`assertThat(...)`) over standard JUnit assertions for better readability.

### gRPC Integration Testing (`@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport`)

* **In-Process Transport:** Annotate gRPC integration tests with `@SpringBootTest` and `@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport` to run the Spring gRPC server in-memory without binding to a network port.
* **Channel & Stub Wiring:** Inject `GrpcChannelFactory` into tests to create channels (`channels.createChannel("local")`) and wrap them with generated `*BlockingStub` clients.
* **Full Pipeline Coverage:** Do not call `*ImplBase` methods directly in integration tests. Always invoke RPCs through a gRPC stub so Protobuf serialization, `ServerInterceptor`s, and exception-to-`io.grpc.Status` mapping are verified end-to-end.
* **Error Assertions:** Assert gRPC error responses using `assertThrows(StatusRuntimeException.class, ...)` and verify both `ex.getStatus().getCode()` and `ex.getStatus().getDescription()`.

#### Reference Test Pattern

```java
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport
class UserGrpcIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired
    private GrpcChannelFactory channels;

    @Test
    void shouldReturnUser_whenValidIdProvided() {
        var stub = UserServiceGrpc.newBlockingStub(channels.createChannel("local"));

        UserResponse response = stub.getUser(
            GetUserRequest.newBuilder().setId("123").build()
        );

        assertThat(response.getName()).isEqualTo("Alice");
    }

    @Test
    void shouldReturnNotFoundStatus_whenUserDoesNotExist() {
        var stub = UserServiceGrpc.newBlockingStub(channels.createChannel("local"));

        StatusRuntimeException ex = assertThrows(StatusRuntimeException.class, () ->
            stub.getUser(GetUserRequest.newBuilder().setId("missing").build())
        );

        assertThat(ex.getStatus().getCode()).isEqualTo(Status.Code.NOT_FOUND);
    }
}
```

**These guidelines are working if:** diffs contain fewer unnecessary changes, fewer rewrites occur due to misunderstood requirements, and clarifying questions happen before implementation rather than after mistakes.

## 12. Agent Execution Checklist

Before finalizing any code generation or modification, verify:

1. [ ] Are all dependencies injected via `private final` fields and a constructor?
2. [ ] Are generated Protobuf classes (`*Request`, `*Response`) and JPA `@Entity` classes completely isolated from the `domain` and `application` layers?
3. [ ] Are gRPC `*ImplBase` classes kept thin, delegating all business rules to application interfaces?
4. [ ] Are exceptions translated to `io.grpc.Status` centrally rather than via repetitive `try-catch` blocks in every RPC method?
5. [ ] Did you avoid speculative abstractions and only touch files directly required by the task?
6. [ ] Are unit tests and `@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport` gRPC stub integration tests included for all new endpoints and business logic?

* **Immutability:** Prefer `final` fields in all Spring beans and use Java `record` types for all internal commands, queries, domain value objects, and `@ConfigurationProperties`.

## 11. Testing Requirements

### Unit & Persistence Tests

* **Unit Tests:** Every new `@Service` and domain component must have fast, isolated unit tests using **JUnit 5** and **Mockito** (no Spring context or gRPC server loaded).
* **Persistence Tests:** Use `@DataJpaTest` and **Testcontainers** for repository integration tests requiring a real database.
* **Assertions:** Prefer **AssertJ** (`assertThat(...)`) over standard JUnit assertions for better readability.

### gRPC Integration Testing (`@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport`)

* **In-Process Transport:** Annotate gRPC integration tests with `@SpringBootTest` and `@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport` to run the Spring gRPC server in-memory without binding to a network port.
* **Channel & Stub Wiring:** Inject `GrpcChannelFactory` into tests to create channels (`channels.createChannel("local")`) and wrap them with generated `*BlockingStub` clients.
* **Full Pipeline Coverage:** Do not call `*ImplBase` methods directly in integration tests. Always invoke RPCs through a gRPC stub so Protobuf serialization, `ServerInterceptor`s, and exception-to-`io.grpc.Status` mapping are verified end-to-end.
* **Error Assertions:** Assert gRPC error responses using `assertThrows(StatusRuntimeException.class, ...)` and verify both `ex.getStatus().getCode()` and `ex.getStatus().getDescription()`.

#### Reference Test Pattern

```java
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport
class UserGrpcIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired
    private GrpcChannelFactory channels;

    @Test
    void shouldReturnUser_whenValidIdProvided() {
        var stub = UserServiceGrpc.newBlockingStub(channels.createChannel("local"));

        UserResponse response = stub.getUser(
            GetUserRequest.newBuilder().setId("123").build()
        );

        assertThat(response.getName()).isEqualTo("Alice");
    }

    @Test
    void shouldReturnNotFoundStatus_whenUserDoesNotExist() {
        var stub = UserServiceGrpc.newBlockingStub(channels.createChannel("local"));

        StatusRuntimeException ex = assertThrows(StatusRuntimeException.class, () ->
            stub.getUser(GetUserRequest.newBuilder().setId("missing").build())
        );

        assertThat(ex.getStatus().getCode()).isEqualTo(Status.Code.NOT_FOUND);
    }
}
```

---

**These guidelines are working if:** diffs contain fewer unnecessary changes, fewer rewrites occur due to misunderstood requirements, and clarifying questions happen before implementation rather than after mistakes.

## 12. Agent Execution Checklist

Before finalizing any code generation or modification, verify:

1. [ ] Are all dependencies injected via `private final` fields and a constructor?
2. [ ] Are generated Protobuf classes (`*Request`, `*Response`) and JPA `@Entity` classes completely isolated from the `domain` and `application` layers?
3. [ ] Are gRPC `*ImplBase` classes kept thin, delegating all business rules to application interfaces?
4. [ ] Are exceptions translated to `io.grpc.Status` centrally rather than via repetitive `try-catch` blocks in every RPC method?
5. [ ] Did you avoid speculative abstractions and only touch files directly required by the task?
6. [ ] Are unit tests and `@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport` gRPC stub integration tests included for all new endpoints and business logic?"}}

---
name: setup-pre-commit
description: Set up Husky pre-commit hooks with lint-staged (Prettier), type checking, and tests in the current repo. Use when user wants to add pre-commit hooks, set up Husky, configure lint-staged, or add commit-time formatting/typechecking/testing.
---

# Setup Pre-Commit Hooks

## What This Sets Up

- **Husky** pre-commit hook
- **lint-staged** running Prettier on all staged files
- **Prettier** config (if missing)
- **typecheck** and **test** scripts in the pre-commit hook

## Steps

### 1. Detect package manager

Check for `package-lock.json` (npm), `pnpm-lock.yaml` (pnpm), `yarn.lock` (yarn), `bun.lockb` (bun). Use whichever is present. Default to npm if unclear.

### 2. Install dependencies

Install as devDependencies:

```
husky lint-staged prettier
```

### 3. Initialize Husky

```bash
npx husky init
```

This creates `.husky/` dir and adds `prepare: "husky"` to package.json.

### 4. Create `.husky/pre-commit`

Write this file (no shebang needed for Husky v9+):

```
npx lint-staged
npm run typecheck
npm run test
```

**Adapt**: Replace `npm` with detected package manager. If repo has no `typecheck` or `test` script in package.json, omit those lines and tell the user.

### 5. Create `.lintstagedrc`

```json
{
  "*": "prettier --ignore-unknown --write"
}
```

### 6. Create `.prettierrc` (if missing)

Only create if no Prettier config exists. Use these defaults:

```json
{
  "useTabs": false,
  "tabWidth": 2,
  "printWidth": 80,
  "singleQuote": false,
  "trailingComma": "es5",
  "semi": true,
  "arrowParens": "always"
}
```

### 7. Verify

- [ ] `.husky/pre-commit` exists and is executable
- [ ] `.lintstagedrc` exists
- [ ] `prepare` script in package.json is `"husky"`
- [ ] `prettier` config exists
- [ ] Run `npx lint-staged` to verify it works

### 8. Commit

Stage all changed/created files and commit with message: `Add pre-commit hooks (husky + lint-staged + prettier)`

This will run through the new pre-commit hooks — a good smoke test that everything works.

## Notes

name: setup-pre-commit
description: Set up Husky pre-commit hooks with lint-staged (Prettier), type checking, and tests in the current repo. Use when user wants to add pre-commit hooks, set up Husky, configure lint-staged, or add commit-time formatting/typechecking/testing.
---

# Setup Pre-Commit Hooks

## What This Sets Up

- **Husky** pre-commit hook
- **lint-staged** running Prettier on all staged files
- **Prettier** config (if missing)
- **typecheck** and **test** scripts in the pre-commit hook

## Steps

### 1. Detect package manager

Check for `package-lock.json` (npm), `pnpm-lock.yaml` (pnpm), `yarn.lock` (yarn), `bun.lockb` (bun). Use whichever is present. Default to npm if unclear.

### 2. Install dependencies

Install as devDependencies:

```
husky lint-staged prettier
```

### 3. Initialize Husky

```bash
npx husky init
```

This creates `.husky/` dir and adds `prepare: "husky"` to package.json.

### 4. Create `.husky/pre-commit`

Write this file (no shebang needed for Husky v9+):

```
npx lint-staged
npm run typecheck
npm run test
```

**Adapt**: Replace `npm` with detected package manager. If repo has no `typecheck` or `test` script in package.json, omit those lines and tell the user.

### 5. Create `.lintstagedrc`

```json
{
  "*": "prettier --ignore-unknown --write"
}
```

### 6. Create `.prettierrc` (if missing)

Only create if no Prettier config exists. Use these defaults:

```json
{
  "useTabs": false,
  "tabWidth": 2,
  "printWidth": 80,
  "singleQuote": false,
  "trailingComma": "es5",
  "semi": true,
  "arrowParens": "always"
}
```

### 7. Verify

- [ ] `.husky/pre-commit` exists and is executable
- [ ] `.lintstagedrc` exists
- [ ] `prepare` script in package.json is `"husky"`
- [ ] `prettier` config exists
- [ ] Run `npx lint-staged` to verify it works

### 8. Commit

Stage all changed/created files and commit with message: `Add pre-commit hooks (husky + lint-staged + prettier)`

This will run through the new pre-commit hooks — a good smoke test that everything works.

## Notes

- Husky v9+ doesn't need shebangs in hook files
- `prettier --ignore-unknown` skips files Prettier can't parse (images, etc.)
- The pre-commit runs lint-staged first (fast, staged-only), then full typecheck and tests

L7: # Introduction 【9†¶】
L8: 
L9: Git hook scripts are useful for identifying simple issues before submission to code review. We run our hooks on every commit to automatically point out issues in code such as missing semicolons, trailing whitespace, and debug statements. By pointing these issues out before code review, this allows a code reviewer to focus on the architecture of a change while not wasting time with trivial style nitpicks.
L10: As we created more libraries and projects we recognized that sharing our pre-commit hooks across projects is painful. We copied and pasted unwieldy bash scripts from project to project and had to manually change the hooks to work for different project structures.
L11: We believe that you should always use the best industry standard linters. Some of the best linters are written in languages that you do not use in your project or have installed on your machine. For example scss-lint is a linter for SCSS written in Ruby. If you’re writing a project in node you should be able to use scss-lint as a pre-commit hook without adding a Gemfile to your project or understanding how to get scss-lint installed.
L12: We built pre-commit to solve our hook issues. It is a multi-language package manager for pre-commit hooks. You specify a list of hooks you want and pre-commit manages the installation and execution of any hook written in any language before every commit. pre-commit is specifically designed to not require root access. If one of your developers doesn’t have node installed but modifies a JavaScript file, pre-commit automatically handles downloading and building node to run eslint without root.
L13: # Installation 【10†¶】
L14: 
L15: Before you can run hooks, you need to have the pre-commit package manager installed.
L16: 
L17: Using pip:
L18: 
L19:     pip install pre-commit
L20: 
L21: 
L22: In a python project, add the following to your requirements.txt (or requirements-dev.txt):

L25: 
L26: 
L27: As a 0-dependency 【11†zipapp†docs.python.org】:
L28: 
L29:   * locate and download the `.pyz` file from the 【12†github releases†github.com】
L30:   * run `python pre-commit-#.#.#.pyz ...` in place of `pre-commit ...`

L32: ## Quick start 【13†¶】
L33: ### 1. Install pre-commit 【14†¶】
L34: 
L35:   * follow the 【2†install】 instructions above
L36:   * `pre-commit --version` should show you what version you're using

L40: ### 2. Add a pre-commit configuration 【15†¶】
L41:   * create a file named `.pre-commit-config.yaml`
L42:   * you can generate a very basic configuration using 【16†`pre-commit sample-config`】
L43:   * the full set of options for the configuration are listed 【3†below】
L44:   * this example uses a formatter for python code, however `pre-commit` works for any programming language
L45:   * other 【17†supported hooks】 are available

L47:     repos:

L92: # Adding pre-commit plugins to your project 【21†¶】
L93: 
L94: Once you have pre-commit installed, adding pre-commit plugins to your project is done with the `.pre-commit-config.yaml` configuration file.
L95: 
L96: Add a file called `.pre-commit-config.yaml` to the root of your project. The pre-commit config file describes what repositories and hooks are installed.
L97: ## .pre-commit-config.yaml - top level 【22†¶】
L98: 【23†`repos`】  | A list of 【24†repository mappings】.
L99: 【25†`default_install_hook_types`】  | (optional: default `[pre-commit]`) a list of `--hook-type`s which will be used by default when running 【26†`pre-commit install`】.
L100: 【27†`default_language_version`】  | (optional: default `{}`) a mapping from language to the default 【28†`language_version`】 that should be used for that language. This will only override individual hooks that do not set 【28†`language_version`】. For example to use `python3.7` for `language: python` hooks:

L102:     default_language_version:
L103:         python: python3.7
L104: 【29†`default_stages`】  | (optional: default (all stages)) a configuration-wide default for the 【30†`stages`】 property of hooks. This will only override individual hooks that do not set 【30†`stages`】. For example:
L105: 
L106:     default_stages: [pre-commit, pre-push]
L107: 【31†`files`】  | (optional: default `''`) global file include pattern.
L108: 【32†`exclude`】  | (optional: default `^$`) global file exclude pattern.
L109: 【33†`fail_fast`】  | (optional: default `false`) set to `true` to have pre-commit stop running hooks after the first failure.
L110: 【34†`minimum_pre_commit_version`】  | (optional: default `'0'`) require a minimum version of pre-commit.

L115:     fail_fast: false

L118: ## .pre-commit-config.yaml - repos 【24†¶】
L119: 
L120: The repository mapping tells pre-commit where to get the code for the hook from.
L121: 
L122: 【35†`repo`】  | the repository url to `git clone` from or one of the special sentinel values: 【36†`local`】, 【37†`meta`】.

L133: ## .pre-commit-config.yaml - hooks 【40†¶】
L134: 
L135: The hook mapping configures which hook from the repository is used and allows for customization. All optional keys will receive their default from the repository's configuration.
L136: 【41†`id`】  | which hook from the repository to use.
L137: 【42†`alias`】  | (optional) allows the hook to be referenced using an additional id when using `pre-commit run <hookid>`.
L138: 【43†`name`】  | (optional) override the name of the hook - shown during hook execution.
L139: 【28†`language_version`】  | (optional) override the language version for the hook. See 【44†Overriding Language Version】.
L140: 【45†`files`】  | (optional) override the default pattern for files to run on.
L141: 【46†`exclude`】  | (optional) file exclude pattern.
L142: 【47†`types`】  | (optional) override the default file types to run on (AND). See 【48†Filtering files with types】.
L143: 【49†`types_or`】  | (optional) override the default file types to run on (OR). See 【48†Filtering files with types】.
L144: 【50†`exclude_types`】  | (optional) file types to exclude.

L146: 【30†`stages`】  | (optional) selects which git hook(s) to run for. See 【52†Confining hooks to run at certain stages】.
L147: 【53†`additional_dependencies`】  | (optional) a list of dependencies that will be installed in the environment where this hook gets run. One useful application is to install plugins for hooks such as `eslint`.

L151: One example of a complete configuration:
L152: 
L153:     repos:
L154:     -   repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks

L160: This configuration says to download the pre-commit-hooks project and run its trailing-whitespace hook.
L161: ## Updating hooks automatically 【57†¶】
L162: 
L163: You can update your hooks to the latest version automatically by running 【58†`pre-commit autoupdate`】. By default, this will bring the hooks to the latest tag on the default branch.
L164: # Usage 【4†¶】

L166: Run `pre-commit install` to install pre-commit into your git hooks. pre-commit will now run on every commit. Every time you clone a project using pre-commit running `pre-commit install` should always be the first thing you do.

L547: ## pre-commit init-templatedir DIRECTORY [options] 【120†¶】
L548: 
L549: Install hook script in a directory intended for use with `git config init.templateDir`.
L550: 
L551: Options:
L552: 
L553:   * `-t HOOK_TYPE, --hook-type HOOK_TYPE`: which hook type to install.
L554: 
L555: Some example useful invocations:
L556: 
L557:     git config --global init.templateDir ~/.git-template
L558:     pre-commit init-templatedir ~/.git-template
L559: 
L560:

L562:

L564: For Windows PowerShell use `$HOME` instead of `~`:

L566:     pre-commit init-templatedir $HOME\.git-template

L961: ## usage with git 2.54+ hook configuration 【160†¶】
L962: 
L963: new in 4.6.0: pre-commit improved support for `git config`-based hooks. a later version will change `pre-commit install` to use this approach.
L964: 
L965: 【161†git 2.54†github.blog】 introduced a new way to install git hook tools via `git config`.
L966: 
L967: the basic gist is the following enables a hook in a git repo:
L968: 
L969:     git config set hook.<name>.event pre-push
L970:     git config set hook.<name>.command 'some command here'
L971: an example setup with `pre-commit` might look like:
L972: 
L973:     # note, the "hook" name here is `pre-commit.pre-commit`
L974:     # for the `pre-commit` "tool" and the `pre-commit` "event"
L975:     git config set hook.pre-commit.pre-commit.event pre-commit
L976:     git config set hook.pre-commit.pre-commit.command 'pre-commit hook-impl --hook-type pre-commit --'
L977: 
L978:     # please follow that naming scheme for future compatibility with `pre-commit install`
L979: 
L980:     # an example with pre-push:
L981:     #
L982:     # git config set hook.pre-commit.pre-push.event pre-push
L983:     # git config set hook.pre-commit.pre-push.command 'pre-commit hook-impl --hook-type pre-push --'
L984: `pre-commit hook-impl` is a "hidden" implementation command with these options:
L985: 
L986:   * `--hook-type ...`: the 【130†hook type】 to use
L987:   * `--config ...`: (optional) path to `.pre-commit-config.yaml`
L988:   * `--skip-on-missing-config`: silently pass when a config is missing
L989: 
L990: some interesting applications of this:
L991: ### "global" installation of pre-commit 【162†¶】
L992: 
L993: with `git config set --global ...` this can automatically enable pre-commit for all repositories:
L994: 
L995:     git config set --global hook.pre-commit.pre-commit.event pre-commit
L996:     git config set --global hook.pre-commit.pre-commit.command 'pre-commit hook-impl --hook-type pre-commit --skip-on-missing-config --'
L997:   * this setup not recommended as it can lead to accidentally running hooks when interacting with an untrusted repository.
L998:   * `--skip-on-missing-config` is recommended here as arbitrary git repositories may not have a `.pre-commit-config.yaml`.
L999: ### always running a hook on all files 【163†¶】
L1000: 
L1001: since you can configure pre-commit as many times as you want you could invoke pre-commit to run a particular hook always and on all files
L1002: 
L1003:     git config set hook.pre-commit.pre-commit-always.event pre-commit
L1004:     git config set hook.pre-commit.pre-commit-always.command 'pre-commit run hookid --hook-stage pre-commit --all-files'
L1005: 
L1006: 
L1007: note: this is not recommended as it has the tendancy to be slow and deviates from the normal expectations of pre-commit.
L1008: ## automatically enabling pre-commit on repositories 【164†¶】
L1009: 
L1010: note: if you are on a new-enough version of `git` you may want to use 【162†this approach】 instead.
L1011: 
L1012: * * *
L1013: 
L1014: `pre-commit init-templatedir` can be used to set up a skeleton for `git`'s `init.templateDir` option. This means that any newly cloned repository will automatically have the hooks set up without the need to run `pre-commit install`.
L1015: To configure, first set `git`'s `init.templateDir` -- in this example I'm using `~/.git-template` as my template directory.
L1016: 
L1017:     $ git config --global init.templateDir ~/.git-template
L1018:     $ pre-commit init-templatedir ~/.git-template
L1019:     pre-commit installed at /home/asottile/.git-template/hooks/pre-commit
L1020: Now whenever you clone a pre-commit enabled repo, the hooks will already be set up!
L1021: 
L1022:     $ git clone -q 【108†[email protected]】:asottile/pyupgrade
L1023:     $ cd pyupgrade
L1024:     $ git commit --allow-empty -m 'Hello world!'
L1025:     Check docstring is first.............................(no files to check)Skipped
L1026:     Check Yaml...........................................(no files to check)Skipped
L1027:     Debug Statements (Python)............................(no files to check)Skipped
L1028:     ...
L1029: `init-templatedir` uses the `--allow-missing-config` option from `pre-commit install` so repos without a config will be skipped:
L1030: 
L1031:     $ git init sample
L1032:     Initialized empty Git repository in /tmp/sample/.git/
L1033:     $ cd sample
L1034:     $ git commit --allow-empty -m 'Initial commit'
L1035:     `.pre-commit-config.yaml` config file not found. Skipping `pre-commit`.
L1036:     [main (root-commit) d1b39c1] Initial commit
L1037: To still require opt-in, but prompt the user to set up pre-commit use a template hook as follows (for example in `~/.git-template/hooks/pre-commit`).
L1038: 
L1039:     #!/usr/bin/env bash

L1050: ## Filtering files with types 【48†¶】
L1051: 
L1052: Filtering with `types` provides several advantages over traditional filtering with `files`.
L1053: 
L1054:   * no error-prone regular expressions
L1055:   * files can be matched by their shebang (even when extensionless)
L1056:   * symlinks / submodules can be easily ignored
L1057: 
L1058: `types` is specified per hook as an array of tags. The tags are discovered through a set of heuristics by the 【165†identify†github.com】 library. `identify` was chosen as it is a small portable pure python library.
L1059: Some of the common tags you'll find from identify:
L1060: 
L1061:   * `file`
L1062:   * `symlink`
L1063:   * `directory` - in the context of pre-commit this will be a submodule
L1064:   * `executable` - whether the file has the executable bit set
L1065:   * `text` - whether the file looks like a text file
L1066:   * `binary` - whether the file looks like a binary file
L1067:   * 【166†tags by extension / naming convention†github.com】
L1068:   * 【167†tags by shebang (`#!`)†github.com】
L1069: To discover the type of any file on disk, you can use `identify`'s cli:
L1070: 
L1071:     $ identify-cli setup.py
L1072:     ["file", "non-executable", "python", "text"]
L1073:     $ identify-cli some-random-file
L1074:     ["file", "non-executable", "text"]
L1075:     $ identify-cli --filename-only some-random-file; echo $?
L1076:     1
L1077: 
L1078: 
L1079: If a file extension you use is not supported, please 【165†submit a pull request†github.com】!
L1080: `types`, `types_or`, and `files` are evaluated together with `AND` when filtering. Tags within `types` are also evaluated using `AND`.
L1081: 
L1082: Tags within `types_or` are evaluated using `OR`.
L1083: 
L1084: For example:
L1085: 
L1086:         files: ^foo/
L1087:         types: [file, python]
L1088: 
L1089: 
L1090: will match a file `foo/1.py` but will not match `setup.py`.
L1091: 
L1092: Another example:
L1093: 
L1094:         files: ^foo/
L1095:         types_or: [javascript, jsx, ts, tsx]

L71: Get high commit message quality and short feedback cycles by linting commit messages right when they are authored.

L113: * * *
L114: ### Using the pre-commit framework 【29†​】

L116: If your project manages its hooks with 【30†pre-commit†pre-commit.com】, add commitlint as a local hook to your `.pre-commit-config.yaml`. pre-commit installs commitlint into an environment of its own, so the project does not need a `package.json`.

L69: # Guide: Local setup 【24†​】
L70: 
L71: Get high commit message quality and short feedback cycles by linting commit messages right when they are authored.
L72: 
L73: This guide demonstrates how to achieve this via git hooks.
L74: 
L75: Follow the 【1†Getting Started】 for basic installation and configuration instructions.
L76: ## Add hook 【25†​】
L77: 
L78: To use commitlint you need to set up a `commit-msg` hook. commitlint runs on the `commit-msg` hook, not on git's `pre-commit` hook.
L79: ### Using a git hooks manager 【26†​】
L80: 
L81: To lint commits before they are created you can use 【27†Husky†typicode.github.io】's `commit-msg` hook.
L82: 
L83: You can find complete setup instructions on the 【28†official documentation†typicode.github.io】.
L84: 
L85: NOTE
L86: 
L87: The following instructions are meant to `husky@v9` if you are using a different version consult the official documentation of your version.
L88: 
L89: * * *
L90: 
L91: [Button: Linux / macOS][Button: Windows]
L92: 
L93: [Button: npm][Button: yarn][Button: pnpm][Button: bun][Button: deno]
L94: sh
L95: 
L96:     `npm install --save-dev husky
L97: 
L98:     # husky@v9
L99:     npx husky init
L100:     # husky@v8 or lower
L101:     npx husky install
L102: 
L103:     # Add commit message linting to commit-msg hook
L104:     echo "npx --no -- commitlint --edit \$1" > .husky/commit-msg`
L105: 
L106: As an alternative you can create a script inside `package.json`
L107: 
L108: sh
L109: 
L110:     `npm pkg set scripts.commitlint="commitlint --edit"
L111:     echo "npm run commitlint \${1}" > .husky/commit-msg`
L112: 
L113: * * *
L114: ### Using the pre-commit framework 【29†​】
L115: 
L116: If your project manages its hooks with 【30†pre-commit†pre-commit.com】, add commitlint as a local hook to your `.pre-commit-config.yaml`. pre-commit installs commitlint into an environment of its own, so the project does not need a `package.json`.
L117: yaml
L118: 
L119:     `default_install_hook_types: [pre-commit, commit-msg]
L120:     default_stages: [pre-commit]
L121:     repos:
L122:       - repo: local
L123:         hooks:
L124:           - id: commitlint
L125:             name: commitlint
L126:             entry: commitlint --edit
L127:             language: node
L128:             stages: [commit-msg]
L129:             additional_dependencies:
L130:               - "@commitlint/cli"
L131:               - "@commitlint/config-conventional"`
L132: 
L133: Then install the hooks:
L134: 
L135: sh
L136: 
L137:     `pre-commit install`
L138: 
L139: NOTE
L140:   * List every package your configuration needs in `additional_dependencies`: shareable configs from `extends`, plugins and parser presets.
L141:   * Pin the versions (for example `"@commitlint/cli@21.2.4"`) for reproducible installs. `pre-commit autoupdate` skips `repo: local` hooks, so bump the versions by hand.
L142:   * commitlint runs on the `commit-msg` hook, so that hook type has to be installed. `default_install_hook_types` takes care of it; without it run `pre-commit install --hook-type commit-msg`.
L143:   * `default_stages: [pre-commit]` keeps your other hooks, the ones that declare no `stages`, from also running on the commit message.
L144: IMPORTANT
L145: 
L146: The hook needs Node.js 22.12 or later. By default pre-commit uses the `node` on your `PATH` only when it is installed outside your home directory. A Node.js from nvm, mise, volta or fnm is ignored, and pre-commit downloads the latest Node.js on the first run instead (on Windows it always downloads). A system Node.js outside your home directory is used as it is, even if it is older than commitlint needs.
L147: Set `language_version` on the hook to choose: `system` uses the `node` on your `PATH`, and a version number such as `22.12.0` makes pre-commit download that version.
L148: 
L149: * * *
L150: ### Using git hooks 【31†​】
L151: 
L152: Info about git hooks can be found on 【32†Git documentation†git-scm.com】.
L153: 
L154: WARNING
L155: 
L156: It's necessary that you use commit-msg as the name for hook file.
L157: 
L158: ## Test 【33†​】
L159: ### Test simple usage 【34†​】
L160: 
L161: For a first simple usage test of commitlint you can do the following:
L162: 
L163: [Input]npm[Input]yarn[Input]pnpm[Input]bun[Input]deno
L164: 
L165: sh
L166: 
L167:     `npx commitlint --from HEAD~1 --to HEAD --verbose`
L168: 
L169: sh
L170: 
L171:     `yarn commitlint --from HEAD~1 --to HEAD --verbose`
L172: 
L173: sh
L174: 
L175:     `pnpm commitlint --from HEAD~1 --to HEAD --verbose`
L176: 
L177: sh
L178: 
L179:     `bun commitlint --from HEAD~1 --to HEAD --verbose`
L180: 
L181: sh
L182: 
L183:     `deno task --eval commitlint --from HEAD~1 --to HEAD --verbose`
L184: This will check your last commit and return an error if invalid or a positive output if valid.
L185: 
L186: TIP
L187: 
L188: To try commitlint without creating a configuration file first, pipe a message to it and use the built-in default config (【35†@commitlint/config-conventional†www.npmjs.com】):
L189: 
L190: sh
L191: 
L192:     `echo "feat: add new feature" | npx commitlint --default-config`
L193: ### Test the hook 【36†​】
L194: 
L195: You can test the hook by simply committing. You should see something like this if everything works.
L196: bash
L197: 
L198:     `git commit -m "foo: this will fail"
L199:     #  husky > commit-msg
L200:     No staged files match any of provided globs.
L201:     ⧗   --- input ---
L202:     foo: this will fail
L203:     ✖   type must be one of [build, chore, ci, docs, feat, fix, perf, refactor, revert, style, test] [type-enum]
L204: 
L205:     ✖   found 1 problems, 0 warnings
L206:     ⓘ   Get help: https://github.com/conventional-changelog/commitlint/#what-is-commitlint
L207: 
L208:     husky - commit-msg script failed (code 1)`
L209: Since 【37†v8.0.0†github.com】 `commitlint` won't output anything if there are no problems with your commit.
L210: (You can use the `--verbose` flag to get positive output)
L211: 
L212: bash
L213: 
L214:     `git commit -m "chore: lint on commitmsg"
L215:     # husky > pre-commit
L216:     No staged files match any of provided globs.
L217:     # husky > commit-msg`
L218: Since 【38†v21.0.0†github.com】 `commitlint` will output the commit message after a new line (EOL) instead of after a colon.
L219: (You can use the `--legacy-output` flag to get the previous output format used in older versions)
L220: 
L221: Local linting is fine for fast feedback but can easily be tinkered with. To ensure all commits are linted you'll want to check commits on an automated CI Server too. Learn how to in the 【4†CI Setup guide】.
